title: Follow a request
summary: System design is deciding how the parts of an application work together. A client asks for something, a service handles the request, and a database keeps information for later.
example: Open a short link → the service finds its saved destination → your browser receives a redirect.
takeaway: Give each part one clear job. Keep important data in durable storage so it survives an application restart.

title: Make room for growth
summary: Scaling means handling more work while keeping a service useful. Vertical scaling makes a machine more powerful. Horizontal scaling adds machines and shares requests across them.
example: At 100 requests per second per server, 250 requests per second need at least 3 servers, assuming traffic is evenly shared.
takeaway: A load balancer distributes requests. Capacity still depends on the slowest shared part, such as the database.

title: Give your database a break
summary: A cache stores a fast, temporary copy of data. A cache hit finds the copy. A cache miss means reading from the original source, often a database.
example: With 1,000 reads per second and an 80% hit rate, only 200 reads per second reach the database.
takeaway: The database remains the source of truth. Cached copies can become stale, so plan how to expire or invalidate them.
